title: Jacob's Last Words to His Twelve Sons
summary: On his deathbed Jacob gathers his sons and speaks a poetic word over each one, telling them what will happen to them in the days to come. Reuben loses the firstborn's place, Simeon and Levi are rebuked for their violence, Judah receives the scepter of rule, and Joseph receives the richest blessing. Jacob then charges his sons to bury him in the cave of Machpelah with Abraham and Isaac, and he dies.
story: Genesis began with God blessing the first humans; it nears its end with a father blessing the twelve sons who will become the twelve tribes of Israel. Jacob has already adopted Joseph's sons (Genesis 48); now he speaks over the whole family. His words look forward, past Egypt, to Israel's life in the land. They explain why the leadership of the family did not go to Reuben, the firstborn, and why it passed to Judah in the south and Joseph in the north, the two great centers of Israel's later history. Jacob's death at the end of the chapter closes the lives of the patriarchs. Only Joseph's story remains to be finished in Genesis 50, and then the family's descendants must wait in Egypt for the promise to be kept.
historical:
The poem is widely regarded as one of the oldest in the Hebrew Bible, alongside the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15) and the Song of Deborah (Judges 5), on the basis of its archaic Hebrew. Traditional readers take it as Jacob's prophecy. Many critical scholars read its sayings as reflecting the circumstances of the tribes in the period of the judges and the early monarchy, with the saying about Judah pointing to David's kingdom around 1000 BC.

The later history of the tribes matches the poem's words at several points. Reuben became a minor tribe east of the Jordan, rebuked in the Song of Deborah for staying by its sheepfolds (Judges 5:15-16). Simeon's inheritance lay inside Judah's territory and was eventually absorbed into it (Joshua 19:1-9). Levi was indeed scattered, but as the priestly tribe living in cities throughout the land (Joshua 21), a change the Bible traces to the Levites' loyalty at the golden calf (Exodus 32:26-29). The tribe of Dan migrated to the far north (Judges 18), and Samson, a Danite, judged Israel. Judah produced Israel's lasting royal house through David. Zebulun's allotment in Joshua 19 lay inland in Galilee, so the saying about the seashore is often taken to describe its access to the coast and its trade rather than an exact border.
cultural:
A father's dying words carried great weight in the ancient world. They were not merely wishes but were believed to shape the future of the sons who heard them, which is why Jacob says he will tell them “what will happen to you in the days to come.” The images come from the life of herders and farmers: a lion over its prey, a strong donkey resting between sheepfolds, a snake by the road, a doe running free, a fruitful vine by a spring, a wolf dividing plunder. The picture of Judah tying his donkey to a vine and washing his clothes in wine (v. 11) is deliberate exaggeration. No one would let a donkey graze on a choice vine unless the vineyard were so abundant that it did not matter.

Jacob's instructions for his burial repeat the details of Abraham's purchase of the cave of Machpelah from Ephron the Hittite (Genesis 23), the only piece of Canaan the family legally owned. To be gathered to one's people was the Hebrew way of speaking about death as joining the ancestors who had gone before.
literary: The chapter is a poem framed by narrative (vv. 1-2 and 28-33). The sons are addressed roughly by their mothers: first Leah's six, then the four sons of the maids, then Rachel's two. The sayings for Judah and Joseph are by far the longest, marking the two tribes that would lead Israel. Several sayings play on the sons' names. Judah sounds like the verb to praise (“your brothers shall praise you”); Dan sounds like the verb to judge or provide justice (v. 16); and the saying about Gad is a string of words built on the sound of his name, meaning raid and raiders. In the middle of the poem Jacob breaks off to pray: “I await Your salvation, O LORD” (v. 18). The Joseph saying (vv. 22-26) piles up names for God: the Mighty One of Jacob, the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel, the God of your father, the Almighty. The narrator's closing note (v. 28) calls the whole poem a blessing, even the harsh words, because each son received what was suitable for him.

outline.t: Dan, and a prayer for salvation

doctrines.note: The saying over Judah promises that the scepter will not depart from him, and that the obedience of the nations will belong to the one who comes from him (v. 10). Jewish and Christian interpreters alike read this as pointing to a coming king, fulfilled first in David and, for Christians, finally in Jesus.

Reuben's incest (35:22) and Simeon and Levi's massacre at Shechem (Genesis 34) are not forgotten. Sin has consequences that reach into later generations. Yet judgment is not the last word even here: Levi's scattering becomes, in time, a priestly calling spread through all Israel.

Jacob's prayer in verse 18, “I await Your salvation, O LORD,” is the first use in the Bible of the Hebrew noun for salvation. In the middle of a poem about his sons' future, the old man confesses that their hope rests not in their strength but in the LORD's deliverance.

words.note: Shevet, a rod or staff, and so a scepter, the symbol of a ruler's authority. The same word also means tribe, since a tribe was a group under one leader's staff. Verse 10 promises that the scepter will not depart from Judah, and verse 16 uses the word for Dan as one of the tribes of Israel. The two senses sit side by side in the poem: the staff of rule is promised to Judah, and the tribes it will one day lead are named all around it.

Yeshu'ah, salvation, deliverance, rescue. Its first appearance in the Bible is Jacob's prayer, “I await Your salvation, O LORD” (v. 18). The word covers rescue from enemies, from danger, and ultimately from sin and death. The name Jesus comes from the Hebrew Yeshua, a form of Joshua, meaning the LORD saves, which is built on the same root.

Acharit, the end, the latter part, the future. Jacob speaks of what will happen in the days to come (v. 1), literally in the end of the days. Here it means the future of the tribes in general, but the same phrase is used by the prophets for the final age of God's purposes (for example Isaiah 2:2), which is one reason interpreters have read parts of this poem as reaching beyond Israel's early history.

christ: The New Testament draws on this chapter directly when it calls the risen Christ “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” (Revelation 5:5), an image from verse 9, and when Hebrews notes that our Lord descended from Judah (Hebrews 7:14). The promise that the scepter will not depart from Judah until the one comes to whom the nations give obedience was read as messianic by ancient Jewish interpreters, and early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr, in the second century, applied verses 10 and 11 to Christ. Many readers also connect the donkey's colt of verse 11 with the prophecy of a humble king riding on a donkey's colt (Zechariah 9:9), which the Gospels see fulfilled as Jesus enters Jerusalem (Matthew 21:5). The poem itself speaks of a ruler from Judah without naming him. Christians confess that the ruler who finally receives the obedience of the nations is Jesus, son of David and son of Judah, whose name means the LORD saves.

hard.q: What does “until Shiloh comes” mean in verse 10?
hard.a:
The Hebrew phrase is one of the most debated in Genesis, and translations differ. One reading, followed by the BSB and the King James tradition, takes Shiloh as a name or title for the coming ruler. A second reading divides the Hebrew letters slightly differently to mean until he comes to whom it belongs, a reading found in some ancient translations, including the Septuagint, and echoed in Ezekiel 21:27, which speaks of the one to whom judgment belongs. A third reading takes the words as until tribute comes to him. A fourth takes Shiloh as the town in Ephraim where the tabernacle stood in the days of the judges, so that the line means until he comes to Shiloh, perhaps referring to the time before Judah's rise.

The first three readings all point to a future ruler from Judah whom the nations will obey, and both the Aramaic translation known as Targum Onkelos and many Christian interpreters read the verse as a promise of the Messiah. The fourth reading is more common among scholars who read the poem as reflecting early tribal history. Whatever the precise wording, the second half of the verse is clear: the allegiance of the nations will belong to the ruler from Judah.

questions: Reuben, Simeon, and Levi hear their past sins named on their father's deathbed. Why can a single night or an outburst of anger shape a whole future, and what does Levi's later story suggest about whether that future is fixed?
In the middle of his words about his sons, Jacob prays, “I await Your salvation, O LORD.” What would it mean for you to wait for God's salvation for people you love whose future you cannot see?
The royal scepter goes to Judah, the brother who proposed selling Joseph. What does that tell you about the kind of people God uses to carry his promises?
